record.paper_title: Some results and open problems in research on low dimensional organic conductors
record.original_question: What physical mechanism explains why, in the Bechgaard salts (TMTSF)2FSO3 and (TMTSF)2ClO4, the anion-ordering temperature increases when external pressure is increased, even though the paper states that simple physical reasoning would suggest the opposite trend? The question concerns salts whose tetrahedral anions can adopt two orientations relative to the crystal lattice, and asks for a plausible microscopic explanation of the observed pressure dependence of the anion-ordering transition.

evidence.quote: Experiments on salts with anions FSO3 and ClO4 have shown that the anion ordering temperature in these two materials increases with the applied pressure [8,9], although simple physical logic would lead to contrary expectations.
To the best of the author’s knowledge no plausible physical explanation of this behaviour has been proposed.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the quasi-one-dimensional organic conductors known as Bechgaard salts of the form (TMTSF)$_2$X, where TMTSF denotes tetramethyltetraselenafulvalene and X is a non-centrosymmetric tetrahedral anion. Focus on the two cases X = FSO$_3$ and X = ClO$_4$. In these crystals each tetrahedral anion can adopt two distinct orientations relative to the surrounding cation lattice, and below a characteristic anion-ordering temperature $T_{AO}$ a structural phase transition occurs in which the anion orientations become long-range ordered, breaking translational symmetry.

A naive thermodynamic/steric argument suggests that applying hydrostatic pressure, which compresses the lattice and reduces the volume available to each anion, should hinder collective reorientation and therefore lower $T_{AO}$. Experimentally, however, in both (TMTSF)$_2$FSO$_3$ and (TMTSF)$_2$ClO$_4$ the anion-ordering temperature $T_{AO}$ is observed to increase as the externally applied hydrostatic pressure is increased.

Problem: Provide a microscopic physical mechanism — based on the coupling between the anion orientational degrees of freedom and the electronic, elastic, or Coulombic degrees of freedom of the TMTSF stacks — that accounts quantitatively, or at least qualitatively, for the observed positive sign of $dT_{AO}/dP$ in these two salts, and explain why this mechanism dominates over the steric reasoning that would predict $dT_{AO}/dP < 0$.
artifact.status_search_result: A web search returned structural and phase-diagram studies of (TMTSF)$_2$ClO$_4$ and related salts, but none of the located sources presents an established microscopic explanation for why the anion-ordering temperature in (TMTSF)$_2$FSO$_3$ and (TMTSF)$_2$ClO$_4$ increases with applied pressure. The status of a generally accepted mechanism is therefore unclear from publicly available results.

status_evidence.title: Temperature and pressure dependencies of the crystal structure of the organic superconductor (TMTSF)2ClO4
status_evidence.snippet: Effects of lowering the temperature are not the same as those produced by increasing the pressure in this compound.
status_evidence.claim: Pressure and temperature act differently on the (TMTSF)2ClO4 lattice, but no microscopic explanation for the positive pressure dependence of T_AO is given.

status_evidence.title: Role of Anion Ordering in the Coexistence of Spin-Density-Wave and Superconductivity in (TMTSF)2ClO4
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses anion ordering and its role in the SDW/superconductivity coexistence, without addressing why dT_AO/dP > 0.
status_evidence.claim: Recent literature focuses on the electronic consequences of anion ordering rather than the sign of its pressure derivative.

status_evidence.title: Structural and Electronic Properties of (TMTTF)2X Salts with Tetrahedral Anions
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews tetrahedral-anion ordering in TMTTF/TMTSF salts.
status_evidence.claim: General reviews of tetrahedral-anion ordering do not provide a definitive mechanism for the positive pressure dependence in FSO3 and ClO4 salts.
